(i) Condensation: two molecules join to form a larger one with elimination of a small molecule (e.g. H2O). Each monomer needs two functional groups (one at each end). Addition polymerization: unsaturated (C=C) monomers join with no loss of any atoms.

  • Disposal problem: most addition polymers are not biodegradable, so take up landfill space for a long time; burning them causes pollution (e.g. HCl from PVC). "Litter" alone is not accepted.

(i) Any two: they make materials (plastics) that do not occur naturally; the materials are chemically unreactive; they have a wide range of uses and properties; they are cheap; they support a large industry; they use a limited natural resource (crude oil).

(ii) Addition polymerization.

(iii) Three repeat units: –CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–, a 6-carbon main chain with a CH3 on every carbon and continuation bonds at both ends.

(iv) Monomers are small molecules with low molar mass and small surface area, so their London (dispersion) forces are weak and little energy is needed to separate them. Polymers are very long chains with much stronger total intermolecular forces, so they are solids.

The other product is water (H₂O), lost as each link forms. The polymer is nylon-6,6.
Poly(chloroethene) (PVC): a chain of six carbons, –CH2–CHCl–CH2–CHCl–CH2–CHCl–, with Cl on alternate carbons and continuation bonds at both ends. Three repeating units of –CH2–CHCl– are required.
The monomer is chloroethene: H2C=CHCl (CH2=CHCl). The double bond must be shown.
Repeating unit: –[CH2–CH(C6H5)]– – two carbons in the backbone, one carrying the benzene ring, with continuation bonds at both ends (no C=C remains).

Polypropene: –CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2–CH(CH3)– , a four-carbon chain with CH3 on alternate carbons and continuation bonds at both ends. The C=C has opened up; the CH3 groups are side branches, not in the chain.
–CH2–CH(C2H5)–CH2–CH(C2H5)–CH2–CH(C2H5)– : a six-carbon backbone with an ethyl branch on alternate carbons and continuation bonds at both ends.
